scenario: You just opened your terminal. Figure out where you are, then look around to see what's in your home directory.

objectives.description: List the contents of the current directory

hints: pwd stands for 'print working directory'
ls lists the contents of a directory
afterSolve: pwd and ls are probably the two commands you'll use most. Try ls -la next time to see hidden files and details.

scenario: Navigate into the projects directory, then into the webapp subdirectory.
hints: Use cd to change directory
You can chain paths: cd projects/webapp
afterSolve: You can navigate multiple levels at once: cd projects/webapp. Or one at a time: cd projects, then cd webapp.

scenario: Your project needs a new configuration file. Create a directory called 'config' inside ~/projects/webapp, then create an empty file called 'settings.json' inside it.
hints: mkdir creates directories
touch creates empty files
afterSolve: mkdir -p can create nested directories in one command: mkdir -p config/sub/deep

scenario: Create a new project structure: a directory called 'api' with two empty files inside it: 'server.py' and 'routes.py'.
hints: First create the directory with mkdir
You can create multiple files at once: touch file1 file2
afterSolve: touch can create multiple files at once. And you can combine: mkdir api && touch api/server.py api/routes.py

scenario: A teammate left notes in a file. Read the contents of ~/projects/webapp/README.md to see what they wrote.

~/projects/webapp/README.md.content:
# Webapp

Run `npm install` then `npm start` to get going.
The API runs on port 3000.

TODO: Add authentication middleware.

hints: cat displays the entire contents of a file
The file is in the current directory
afterSolve: For long files, use head -n 10 to see just the first 10 lines, or tail -n 5 for the last 5.

scenario: There's a long log file. You only need to see the last 3 lines to check the most recent entries.

~/projects/webapp/app.log.content:
2024-01-15 08:00:01 INFO Server started on port 3000
2024-01-15 08:05:12 INFO GET /api/users 200
2024-01-15 08:05:13 INFO GET /api/posts 200
2024-01-15 08:10:44 WARN Slow query detected (2.3s)
2024-01-15 08:12:01 ERROR Connection to database lost
2024-01-15 08:12:05 INFO Reconnecting to database...
2024-01-15 08:12:06 INFO Database connection restored

objectives.description: Show the last 3 lines of app.log

hints: tail shows the end of a file
Use -n to specify how many lines
afterSolve: tail -f follows a file in real-time — super useful for watching logs as they update.

scenario: You're in ~/projects/webapp. Without changing directory, display the contents of the README.md file that's in the parent directory (~/projects).

~/projects/README.md.content:
# Projects
This directory contains all active projects.

objectives.description: Read the README.md from the parent directory without leaving webapp

validation.expected: This directory contains all active projects

hints: .. refers to the parent directory
cat ../README.md would read a file one level up
afterSolve: Relative paths save time. ../file.txt goes up one level. ../../file.txt goes up two.

scenario: You want to learn what options the ls command supports. Use the manual to find out.

objectives.description: Look up the manual for ls

hints: man followed by a command name shows its manual
Alternatively, many commands support --help
afterSolve: man pages are your reference guide. Use which to find where a command lives: which python3

scenario: Make a backup of the config file before editing it. Copy ~/projects/webapp/config.json to ~/projects/webapp/config.json.bak.

objectives.description: Create a backup copy of config.json

hints: cp copies files: cp source destination
The .bak extension is a convention for backup files
afterSolve: Always back up config files before editing. cp -r copies entire directories recursively.

scenario: Reorganize: move the utils.py file from the root of the project into the lib directory.

objectives.description: Move utils.py into the lib directory

hints: mv moves (or renames) files: mv source destination
mv utils.py lib/ moves it into the lib directory
afterSolve: mv also renames files: mv old_name.py new_name.py. It's the same command for both operations.

scenario: Clean up: remove the temp directory and everything inside it. Then verify it's gone by listing the current directory.

objectives.description: Remove the temp directory and its contents

hints: rm removes files, but for directories you need the -r flag
rm -r temp removes the directory and everything inside it
afterSolve: rm -r is irreversible — there's no trash can. Use rm -ri for interactive confirmation on each file.

scenario: Find all Python files (.py) in the projects directory. You need to know what scripts exist across all subdirectories.
hints: find searches for files: find <path> -name <pattern>
Use quotes around the pattern: find . -name '*.py'
afterSolve: find is extremely powerful. Add -type f for files only, -type d for directories only.

scenario: Your app is throwing an error but you're not sure which file contains the problematic import. Search for the word 'database' across all files in the project.

~/projects/webapp/app.py.content:
from flask import Flask
from database import connect_db

app = Flask(__name__)

hints: grep searches for text patterns in files
Use -r to search recursively and -i for case-insensitive
afterSolve: grep -rn adds line numbers to results. grep -ri 'pattern' . searches everything in the current directory.

scenario: You've written a deploy script but can't run it because it doesn't have execute permission. Make deploy.sh executable.
hints: chmod changes file permissions
chmod +x adds execute permission
afterSolve: chmod +x is the most common permission change. Octal notation (chmod 755) gives finer control: owner=rwx, group=rx, others=rx.

scenario: Save a list of all files in the current project to a file called 'filelist.txt'. Use output redirection.

objectives.description: Redirect a file listing into filelist.txt

hints: > redirects output to a file: command > file.txt
ls > filelist.txt would save the listing
afterSolve: > overwrites the file. >> appends to it. Useful for building up log files: echo 'entry' >> log.txt

scenario: Count how many JavaScript files exist in the src directory. Use a pipe to combine find and wc.
hints: Pipes connect the output of one command to the input of another: cmd1 | cmd2
find . -name '*.js' | wc -l counts the results
afterSolve: Pipes are the backbone of shell power. Chain as many as you need: find | grep | sort | uniq | wc

scenario: You have a log file with duplicate entries. Sort the entries and remove duplicates to get a clean list.

~/projects/errors.log.content:
ConnectionError: timeout
ValueError: invalid input
ConnectionError: timeout
KeyError: missing_key
ValueError: invalid input
TypeError: expected string
ConnectionError: timeout
KeyError: missing_key

objectives.description: Sort the log and remove duplicate lines

hints: sort orders lines alphabetically
uniq removes consecutive duplicate lines (so sort first, then uniq)
Or use sort -u to do both at once
afterSolve: uniq -c prepends a count to each line — great for finding the most common errors.

scenario: Count the number of lines, words, and characters in the README file.

~/projects/webapp/README.md.content:
# My Webapp

A full-stack web application built with React and Flask.

## Getting Started

1. Install dependencies: npm install
2. Start the server: npm start
3. Open http://localhost:3000

objectives.description: Get line, word, and character counts for README.md

hints: wc (word count) gives you lines, words, and characters
Just run wc on the file — no flags needed for all three counts
afterSolve: wc -l for lines only, wc -w for words only. Combine with pipes: cat file | wc -l

scenario: Something is using port 3000 and your dev server can't start. List running processes to find what's running, then kill the process with PID 1234.
hints: ps shows running processes. ps aux shows all processes
kill PID sends a termination signal to a process
afterSolve: kill -9 PID force-kills a stubborn process. lsof -i :3000 finds what's using a specific port.

scenario: Set an environment variable called DATABASE_URL to 'postgres://localhost/myapp', then verify it's set by printing it.
hints: export sets environment variables: export VAR=value
echo $VAR prints a variable's value
afterSolve: Environment variables set with export only last for the current session. Add them to ~/.zshrc to make them permanent.

scenario: Create an alias called 'gs' that runs 'git status'. Then use your new alias.
hints: alias name='command' creates a shortcut
alias gs='git status' — then just type gs
afterSolve: Add aliases to ~/.zshrc to keep them permanent. Oh My Zsh's git plugin comes with tons of built-in aliases.

scenario: Initialize a new Node.js project and install Express as a dependency.
hints: npm init creates a package.json. Use -y to skip questions
npm install express adds express as a dependency
afterSolve: npm i is shorthand for npm install. Use --save-dev (or -D) for dev-only dependencies like linters and test frameworks.

scenario: Create a Python virtual environment called 'venv' and activate it.
hints: python3 -m venv venv creates a virtual environment
source venv/bin/activate activates it
afterSolve: Always use virtual environments for Python projects to isolate dependencies. deactivate exits the venv.

scenario: Initialize a new git repository, stage all files, and make your first commit with the message 'initial commit'.
hints: git init creates a new repository
git add . stages all files
git commit -m 'message' makes a commit
afterSolve: git status is your best friend — run it between operations to understand what's staged and what's not.

scenario: Check the status of your repository, then view the commit history to see recent changes.
hints: git status shows what's changed
git log shows commit history
afterSolve: git log --oneline gives a compact view. git log --graph shows branch topology.

scenario: Create a new branch called 'feature/auth' and switch to it.

objectives.description: Create and switch to the feature/auth branch

hints: git checkout -b creates and switches to a new branch in one step
Or use git branch name + git checkout name as two steps
afterSolve: git switch is the modern alternative to checkout for switching branches. git switch -c creates and switches.

scenario: Generate a new SSH key pair for GitHub. Use the ed25519 algorithm and your email 'dev@startup.com'.

objectives.description: Generate an SSH key with ed25519

hints: ssh-keygen generates SSH key pairs
Use -t ed25519 for the algorithm and -C for a comment/email
afterSolve: After generating, add the key to the ssh-agent: eval $(ssh-agent) && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

scenario: List all running Docker containers, then check which Docker images are available locally.
hints: docker ps lists running containers
docker images lists downloaded images
afterSolve: docker ps -a shows ALL containers (including stopped ones). docker system prune cleans up unused resources.

scenario: Test your local API by sending a GET request to http://localhost:3000/api/health.

objectives.description: Send a GET request to the health endpoint

hints: curl sends HTTP requests from the terminal
curl http://localhost:3000/api/health
afterSolve: curl -v shows verbose headers. curl -X POST -d '{"key":"val"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' sends POST data.

scenario: Send a POST request to http://localhost:3000/api/users with JSON body '{"name": "Alice"}'. Include the Content-Type header.

objectives.description: Send a POST request with JSON body

hints: Use -X POST to specify the HTTP method
Use -H 'Content-Type: application/json' for the header and -d for the body
afterSolve: httpie (http command) is a friendlier alternative: http POST localhost:3000/api/users name=Alice

scenario: Write a command that loops through all .py files in the current directory and prints their names.

objectives.description: Use a for loop to iterate over .py files

hints: Shell for loops: for f in *.py; do echo $f; done
The glob *.py matches all Python files in the current directory
afterSolve: Shell loops are one-liners with semicolons. Or write multi-line scripts in .sh files for complex logic.

scenario: You need to apply a specific commit from another branch. Cherry-pick commit abc1234 into your current branch.
hints: git cherry-pick <commit-hash> applies a specific commit to your current branch
Just provide the commit hash
afterSolve: Cherry-pick is great for hotfixes. If there's a conflict, resolve it and run git cherry-pick --continue.

scenario: Start all services defined in docker-compose.yml in detached mode, then check their status.

~/projects/webapp/docker-compose.yml.content:
version: '3'
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
  db:
    image: postgres:14
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret

objectives.description: Check the status of running services

hints: docker compose up -d starts services in the background
docker compose ps shows their status
afterSolve: docker compose logs -f follows the logs. docker compose down stops and removes everything.

scenario: Replace all occurrences of 'localhost' with '0.0.0.0' in config.json using sed.

objectives.description: Use sed to replace localhost with 0.0.0.0

hints: sed 's/old/new/g' replaces text. g means global (all occurrences)
sed 's/localhost/0.0.0.0/g' config.json
afterSolve: On macOS, use sed -i '' for in-place editing. On Linux it's sed -i. The empty quotes are a macOS quirk.

scenario: Find out what process is using port 8080. Use lsof to investigate.
hints: lsof -i :PORT shows what's using a specific port
lsof stands for 'list open files' — in Unix, everything is a file, including network connections
afterSolve: Combine with kill: lsof -ti :8080 | xargs kill. The -t flag outputs just the PID.

scenario: Look up the IP address of github.com using a DNS query tool.
hints: dig performs DNS lookups
dig github.com shows the DNS records for a domain
afterSolve: dig +short gives just the IP. nslookup is the simpler alternative. These are essential for debugging network issues.

scenario: Write a one-liner that checks if a file called 'app.py' exists in the current directory and prints a message accordingly.

objectives.description: Use an if statement to check if app.py exists

hints: if [ -f file ]; then ... fi checks if a file exists
-f tests for a regular file, -e tests for existence of any type
afterSolve: Other useful tests: -d (directory exists), -r (readable), -w (writable), -x (executable), -s (file is non-empty).
